chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, and others, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalat, from Al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from Sama'ah, from Abu Baseer, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about a man who prayed but did not know whether he was in the third or the fourth (rak'ah). He (peace be upon him) said: 'Whatever his guess (wahm) leads him to, if he thinks he is in the third and has some notion in his heart of the fourth, he should give the greeting of peace (salam) to himself and his own self, then he should pray two rak'ahs, reciting in them with the Opening of the Book (Al-Fatihah).'

key_terms.سَلَّمَ: He gave the greeting of peace (salam), concluding the prayer.
key_terms.فَاتِحَةُ الْكِتَابِ: The Opening of the Book, referring to Surah Al-Fatihah.
key_terms.وَهْمٌ: Intuition or guesswork; a mental inclination without certainty.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a worshipper who is unsure if they are in the third or fourth rak'ah of prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes the principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) in Shia jurisprudence, where the default assumption is that the prayer is complete unless proven otherwise. By relying on *wahm* (psychological inclination), the worshipper validates the third rak'ah and performs two additional *Qada* (compensatory) rak'ahs, a ruling distinct from the Sunni practice of *Sujud al-Sahw* (prostration of forgetfulness). This method ensures the validity of the prayer while addressing the uncertainty through a specific act of compensation rather than immediate correction.
